titles.title: How far does a random forest generalize from a 54-run LAMMPS+SPICA benchmark?

descriptions.description: Selecting near-optimal hybrid MPI+OpenMP configurations for molecular dynamics workloads on modern HPC clusters has traditionally required exhaustive empirical benchmarking, consuming allocation budget proportional to the number of configurations evaluated. This work investigates whether a cold-start Random Forest surrogate, trained once on a small, structured benchmark dataset, can reliably predict execution performance and recommend high-performing configurations without further cluster runs. The training dataset comprises 54 LAMMPS+SPICA runs of the antimicrobial peptide Tritrpticin on a hydrated DOPC bilayer (4 354 coarse-grained beads), spanning 18 hybrid configurations on 1-8 AMD EPYC 7662 nodes of the Lovelace cluster at CENAPAD-SP, with three independent replications each. Nine topology and resource features feed five regressors that predict loop time and four internal LAMMPS timing fractions (Pair, Kspace, Comm, Modify). In-sample mean absolute error is 0.49 s on loop time (4.0 % relative). Feature importance localizes predictive signal in topology variables (OpenMP threads and MPI/OpenMP ratio dominate; raw node and core counts contribute under 3 %). Leave-one-dimension-out generalization reveals that accuracy is governed by hardware regime membership: within a common regime (single-node, multi-node, or shared threading tier) the surrogate ranks configurations correctly, and degrades when targets cross architectural boundaries. The result is an interpretable map of where the surrogate's recommendations can be trusted, useful for scoping further benchmark campaigns at a fraction of their nominal cost.

titles.title: Functionalisation data of a carbon electrode biosensor for detection of antimicrobial resistance

attributes.publisher: NERC EDS Environmental Information Data Centre

affiliation: NERC EDS Environmental Information Data Centre
contributors.name: NERC EDS Environmental Information Data Centre

descriptions.description: The dataset consists of results of the electrochemical circle fit of the Nyquist plot generated by NOVA software to measure the Charge Transfer Resistance (RCT). Data demonstrates the curve of real and imaginary resistance against charges transmitted in the media of the carbon electrode biosensor. The change in RCT can detect the presence of the targeted antimicrobial resistance (AMR) DNA. The experiments were conducted by immersing the sensor's electrode in different concentrations of the target AMR DNA to determine the limit of detection.

The fabrication process involves multi LTCC layers, and screen printing of silver reference electrode (RE), carbon layer of working electrode (WE) and counter electrode (CE), and the dielectric layers. The SPCEs were functionalised with a specific (Peptide nucleic acid)  PNA probe, by electrografting through in situ generated diazonium cations. Then creating a 4-carboxyphenyl (AP) film on the electrode surface after the modification of SPCEs electrochemical by reduction of the in situ generated 4-carboxyphenyl diazonium salt, using four cyclic voltammetry (CV) scans from +0.4 to -0.6 V at a scan rate of 100mV/s. The AP film then activated via 60 min incubation in 1-Ethyl-3-(3-Dimethylaminopropyl)Carbodiimide (EDC) and NHS (N-hydroxysuccinimide) in a MES (2-(Nmorpholino) EthaneSulfonic acid), PH 5.0. After, the electrode surface rinsed in MES buffer, and incubated it in amino-modified PNA probe dispersed in droplet of PBS buffer for 60 min at room temperature. Formation of a blocking film by droplet deposition to the electrode of 1% v/v ethanolamine/PBS buffer and incubated for 30 min in room temperature. Finaly, 52 min incubation with complimentary DNA target and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements by (Metrohm-Autolab, PGSTAT204/FRA32M), (dRCT 100kHz to 0.3Hz) in a 1mM KCl + 2mM Ferri/Ferrocyanide solution. DNA strand hybridizing to probs lead to an accumulation of negative charge on the electrode surface causing an increase in the charge transfer resistance (RCT).

titles.title: PETAL (Pattern-Enforced Transformer for Antimicrobial peptide Learning)

descriptions.description:
PETAL (Pattern-Enforced Transformer for Antimicrobial peptide Learning) is a generative AI pipeline for de novo design of antimicrobial peptides against Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA persisters and biofilms. The pipeline integrates a GPT-style language model with dual random forest regressors to generate, score, and rank novel peptide candidates by predicted therapeutic index before synthesis and experimental testing.

The repository contains two components. PETAL-GPT is a causal transformer (~207,000 parameters) trained on 1,831 S. aureus-active peptide sequences from the Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP). It generates novel 12-mer candidates across nine configurations spanning three amino acid series (PETAL-N, PETAL-E, PETAL-A) and three net positive charge targets (+2, +3, +4) using a pattern-biased decoding strategy with adaptive relaxation. PETAL-TI trains two independent random forest regressors — one for antimicrobial potency (log₂ MIC against S. aureus, n = 3,779 sequences) and one for mammalian cell toxicity (log₂ CC50/HC50, n = 905 sequences) — and combines predictions into a therapeutic index score to rank candidates by predicted selectivity.

This release accompanies the manuscript: "PETAL: A Generative AI Framework for De Novo Design of Potent and Selective Antimicrobial Peptides Against MRSA Persisters and Biofilms." Houston Methodist Research Institute.

titles.title: OmegAMP: Targeted AMP Discovery via Biologically Informed Generation

descriptions.description: Deep learning-based antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery faces critical challenges such as limited controllability, lack of representations that efficiently model antimicrobial properties, and low experimental hit rates. To address these challenges, we introduce OmegAMP, a framework designed for reliable AMP generation with increased controllability. Its diffusion-based generative model leverages a novel conditioning mechanism to achieve fine-grained control over desired physicochemical properties and to direct generation towards specific activity profiles, including species-specific effectiveness. This is further enhanced by a biologically informed encoding space that significantly improves overall generative performance. Complementing these generative capabilities, OmegAMP leverages a novel synthetic data augmentation strategy to train classifiers for AMP filtering, drastically reducing false positive rates and thereby increasing the likelihood of experimental success. Our in silico experiments demonstrate that OmegAMP delivers state-of-the-art performance across key stages of the AMP discovery pipeline, enabling us to achieve an unprecedented success rate in wet lab experiments. We tested 25 candidate peptides, 24 of them (96%) demonstrated antimicrobial activity, proving effective even against multi-drug resistant strains. Our findings underscore OmegAMP's potential to significantly advance computational frameworks in the fight against antimicrobial resistance.

titles.title: Development of antisense peptide nucleic acid strategies and a novel geometric viability assay for combating major enteric pathogens

rightsList.rights: All items in eScholarship@McGill are protected by copyright with all rights reserved unless otherwise indicated.

descriptions.description: Xin Zhao (Supervisor)

This thesis addresses the escalating challenges of antibiotic resistance and foodborne illnesses in the poultry industry by developing targeted antisense peptide nucleic acid (PNA) therapeutics and establishing a novel high-throughput platform for resistance detection and viability assessment. In light of the growing public health concern due to multidrug-resistant Salmonella enterica, our research proposes innovative antibacterial strategy: a bactericidal approach that targets essential genes critical for bacterial growth and replication. Utilizing a systematic review of the current literature, we established design parameters for effective PNA constructs, emphasizing factors such as construct length, binding site selection, and conjugation with cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs). Our in-vitro investigations demonstrated that CPP-PNA conjugates effectively downregulate gene expression, resulting in significant growth inhibition of Salmonella, as evidenced by a dose-dependent reduction in colony-forming units. Complementary morphological analyses revealed that antisense-mediated gene knockdown disrupts cellular division and elongation processes in the bacterium. In vivo studies using a Caenorhabditis elegans infection model validated the efficacy and safety of the optimized PNA constructs, showing significant improvements in survival rates upon treatment.Concurrently, to address the need for rapid antimicrobial sensitivity assessment, we introduced an innovative Geometric Viability Assay (GVA) for anaerobic bacteria, which provided rapid, reliable, and cost-effective viability assessments with a dynamic range extending over five orders of magnitude. This assay not only matched the performance of traditional plate-based methods but also demonstrated utility in antibiotic sensitivity testing and spore quantification, thereby enhancing its applicability in both research and clinical settings.Overall, our findings substantiate the potential of tailored antisense PNA therapeutics as a precision antimicrobial strategy that circumvents the limitations of conventional antibiotics, while the development of the GVA provides a critical diagnostic and assessment tool to support such interventions. By integrating advanced therapeutic design with a robust detection methodology, this research offers valuable contributions to the fight against antibiotic resistance and paves the way for novel interventions in the post-antibiotic era.

Cette thèse aborde les défis croissants liés à la résistance aux antibiotiques et aux maladies d'origine alimentaire dans l'industrie avicole en développant des thérapies ciblées à base d'acides nucléiques peptidiques antisens (PNA) et en mettant en place une nouvelle plateforme à haut débit pour la détection de la résistance et l'évaluation de la viabilité. Compte tenu des préoccupations croissantes en matière de santé publique liées à la Salmonella enterica multirésistante, notre recherche propose une stratégie antibactérienne innovante : une approche bactéricide qui cible les gènes essentiels à la croissance et à la réplication bactériennes. À partir d'une revue systématique de la littérature actuelle, nous avons établi des paramètres de conception pour des constructions PNA efficaces, en mettant l'accent sur des facteurs tels que la longueur de la construction, la sélection du site de liaison et la conjugaison avec des peptides pénétrant les cellules (CPP). Nos recherches in vitro ont démontré que les conjugués CPP-PNA régulent efficacement l'expression génétique, ce qui entraîne une inhibition significative de la croissance de Salmonella, comme le prouve la réduction dose-dépendante des unités formant colonie. Des analyses morphologiques complémentaires ont révélé que l'inhibition génique médiée par l'antisens perturbe les processus de division et d'élongation cellulaires chez la bactérie. Des études in vivo utilisant un modèle d'infection par Caenorhabditis elegans ont validé l'efficacité et la sécurité des constructions PNA optimisées, montrant des améliorations significatives des taux de survie après traitement.Parallèlement, afin de répondre au besoin d'une évaluation rapide de la sensibilité aux antimicrobiens, nous avons introduit un test de viabilité géométrique (GVA) innovant pour les bactéries anaérobies, qui a permis d'obtenir des évaluations de viabilité rapides, fiables et rentables avec une gamme dynamique s'étendant sur cinq ordres de grandeur. Ce test a non seulement égalé les performances des méthodes traditionnelles basées sur des plaques, mais a également démontré son utilité dans les tests de sensibilité aux antibiotiques et la quantification des spores, renforçant ainsi son applicabilité dans les domaines de la recherche et de la clinique.Dans l'ensemble, nos résultats confirment le potentiel des thérapies antisens PNA sur mesure en tant que stratégie antimicrobienne de précision qui contourne les limites des antibiotiques conventionnels, tandis que le développement du GVA fournit un outil de diagnostic et d'évaluation essentiel pour soutenir ces interventions. En intégrant une conception thérapeutique avancée à une méthodologie de détection robuste, cette recherche apporte une contribution précieuse à la lutte contre la résistance aux antibiotiques et ouvre la voie à de nouvelles interventions dans l'ère post-antibiotique.

titles.title: Hormonal Drivers of Perimenopausal Inflammation and Mood Symptoms

descriptions.description:
Up to one third of women, up to a billion people, experience the emergence or worsening of depressive
and anxiety (mood) symptoms as their hormonal milieu shifts into perimenopause. Despite this proportion, we
still do not understand what biological changes in perimenopause contribute to the increased risk of symptoms.
Recent work suggests that perimenopause initiates a proinflammatory state and links both follicle-stimulating
hormone (FSH) and acyl-ghrelin, two peripheral hormones that can cross the blood-brain barrier, to negative
health outcomes. The roles of FSH and acyl-ghrelin extend beyond their canonical links to fertility and hunger,
respectively. FSH receptors and ghrelin receptors are observed in many tissues and cells, including immune
cells. FSH receptors are highly expressed in monocytes and FSH receptor activation stimulates proinflammatory
cytokine production. Ghrelin receptors are expressed in the efferent vagus nerve, a well-known anti-inflammatory
component of the autonomic nervous system, and acyl-ghrelin signaling increases vagal activity. Despite these
observations, the hormonal mechanisms leading to mood symptoms remain elusive because the convergent
hormonal pathways linking perimenopausal inflammation and mood symptoms have not been modeled.
 Our goal is to compare the time course of changes in FSH, estradiol, other reproductive hormones and
acyl-ghrelin with the time course of changes in inflammation and mood. The study tests a mechanistic hypothesis
in which elevated FSH and decreased acyl-ghrelin elevate proinflammatory markers through actions on
monocytes and the autonomic nervous system, and thereby increase depressive and anxiety symptoms. This
is a prospective longitudinal case-control study using a surgical menopause model, i.e. risk-reducing bilateral
salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO). Surgical menopause reduces inter-individual variation in the onset and duration
of perimenopause, thus facilitating our ability to measure associations between hormones, inflammation, and
vagal activity pre- and post-menopause. We will recruit women seeking premenopausal risk-reducing BSO and
age-matched premenopausal “controls” having non-BSO gynecological surgery. We will collect endocrine,
immune and other measures pre-surgery, one week post-surgery and monthly post-surgery up to six months.
 Aim 1 will test the hypothesis that mood symptoms change with surgical menopause and that changes
in hormones and proinflammatory markers relate to mood symptoms, specifically measuring plasma levels of
FSH, estradiol, acyl-ghrelin, progesterone, liver-enriched antimicrobial peptide 2, cytokines and adipokines in
basal plasma. Aim 2 will test the hypothesis that proinflammatory markers change with surgical menopause and
that changes in acyl-ghrelin and vagal activity (vagal reflex, heart rate variability) relate to proinflammatory
markers. Aim 3 (exploratory) will test the hypothesis that hormones relate to monocyte signaling changes with
surgical menopause and that this signaling relates to proinflammatory markers. Mediation models will test for
mechanistic effects across all aims.

titles.title: Raw data for manuscript entitle Proteomic and Lipidomic Characterization of Hemipyrellia ligurriens Larval Extracts Using LC-MS/MS and GC-MS: Identification of Putative Antimicrobial Molecules and Preliminary Functional Assessment

descriptions.description: Hemipyrellia ligurriens is a tropical Old-World blow fly (Diptera: Calliphoridae) of medical and forensic importance whose larval molecular biology has remained largely uncharacterised. This dataset provides the first label-free LC-MS/MS proteomic comparison of whole-body extracts (WE) and excretory–secretory (ES) products from third-instar larvae of this species. WE were prepared by methanolic homogenisation of 400 third-instar larvae (~10 g); ES products were collected by a 60-min sterile-water incubation of 2,000 third-instar larvae. Peptides were analysed on a Dionex UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano coupled to a Bruker Q-ToF Compact mass spectrometer. Raw spectra were processed with MaxQuant v1.6.2.10 plus the Andromeda search engine against the UniProt Calliphoridae database at 1 % false-discovery rate at both peptide-spectrum-match and protein-group levels with label-free quantitation (LFQ) and the 'match between runs' option enabled. Putatively identified proteins (9,444 in WE, 10,977 in ES; 7,896 shared) and the < 20 kDa antimicrobial / immune-effector subset are reported in the associated PLOS ONE manuscript.

titles.title: Expanding the amyloid landscape: structural plasticity of antimicrobial peptides

descriptions.description: Amyloid formation is increasingly recognized as a functional property of antimicrobial and virulence-associated peptides, yet the relationship between peptide assembly, structure, and biological activity remains poorly understood. Here, we combined computational prediction with biophysical, functional, native mass spectrometry, and cryo-EM analyses to identify fifteen previously unrecognized fibril-forming peptides and define their assembly landscapes. Most peptides displayed pronounced structural plasticity, undergoing environmentally induced transitions between α-helical and β-rich conformations. High-resolution cryo-EM structures of aurein 1.2 and brevinin-1OKc revealed multiple polymorphic cross-β architectures, including a distinctive radially symmetric six-pointed assembly, while native mass spectrometry uncovered fundamentally different oligomerization pathways despite convergence on cross-β fibrillar endpoints. Together, these findings support a model in which biological activity is governed not by a single structural endpoint but by transitions across a dynamic assembly landscape containing multiple accessible amyloid states and soluble intermediates. Our results establish structural plasticity as a defining feature of antimicrobial and virulence-associated peptides and suggest that environmentally regulated transitions across an amyloid assembly landscape provide a mechanism for rapid functional adaptation.

titles.title: Dataset and trained models for Gated Modulation Protein Language Model for Prediction of Antimicrobial Peptide Activity

descriptions.description:
This dataset supplements our research work entitled “Gated Protein Language Modeling for Accurate Prediction of Antimicrobial Peptide Activity.”

The database follows the directory structure described below:

five_fold_ecoli:Computational datasets constructed for model training, stored in .pkl format.

five_fold_s_aureus:Five-fold cross-validation datasets for Staphylococcus aureus.

 

five_fold_p_aeruginosa: 

Five-fold cross-validation datasets for P. Aeruginosa 

embed:Residue-level peptide embeddings for E. coli and S. aureus and P. aeruginosa peptides computed using Protein Language models..

grampa.csv:The original peptide sequence database containing antimicrobial peptides across multiple bacterial species, including E. coli, P. Aeruginosa, and S. aureus. All derived datasets were constructed from this base file.

The original grampa.csv dataset is attributed to the study:

Deep learning regression model for antimicrobial peptide designhttps://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/692681v1.full

titles.title: Hypothesis LL-37, Plasmin, and PAI-1: A Ratchet Model of Chronic Pain, Sepsis Susceptibility, and Fibrinolytic Entrenchment

descriptions.description:
Abstract

We propose a unified mechanistic framework connecting the antimicrobial peptide LL-37, the fibrinolytic system, and protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR2)-mediated nociception into a ratcheting attractor model of chronic inflammation. LL-37, released in response to tissue harm, drives plasminogen activation via the uPA/uPAR axis, elevating plasmin. Plasmin serves dual functions: ECM clearance and specialised pro-resolving mediator (SPM) production, and direct nociceptor sensitisation via PAR2. Counter-regulatory PAI-1 elevation suppresses plasmin between harm episodes but fails to clear fully under chronic or repeated insult, producing per-cycle ratcheting of PAI-1 toward an entrenched ceiling. At ceiling, the system maintains sufficient residual plasmin for sustained PAR2 tone and chronic pain, while insufficient plasmin prevents ECM resolution or SPM generation — creating a dual neurological and fibrinolytic attractor. When infection occurs in this entrenched state, compressed fibrinolytic dynamic range converts an ordinarily self-limiting inflammatory response into an escalating LL-37-driven loop with sepsis-like characteristics. Genetic predisposition via the SERPINE1 4G/4G polymorphism establishes elevated PAI-1 baseline, accelerating ratchet progression. Chronic inflammation progressively demethylates the SERPINE1 promoter via TNF-alpha/TET1 signalling, epigenetically entrenching high PAI-1 expression independently of ongoing inflammatory stimulus. Aspirin's therapeutic action is reframed as phase-dependent ratchet interruption: AT-SPMs generated by acetylated COX-2 directly suppress PAI-1, restoring transient plasmin-mediated resolution capacity. The framework generates specific falsifiable predictions distinguishing it from existing models and identifies SERPINE1 methylation status as a candidate stratification biomarker for sepsis risk in chronically inflamed patient

titles.title: Hypothesis LL-37, Plasmin, and PAI-1: A Ratchet Model of Chronic Pain, Sepsis Susceptibility, and Fibrinolytic Entrenchment

descriptions.description:
Abstract

We propose a unified mechanistic framework connecting the antimicrobial peptide LL-37, the fibrinolytic system, and protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR2)-mediated nociception into a ratcheting attractor model of chronic inflammation. LL-37, released in response to tissue harm, drives plasminogen activation via the uPA/uPAR axis, elevating plasmin. Plasmin serves dual functions: ECM clearance and specialised pro-resolving mediator (SPM) production, and direct nociceptor sensitisation via PAR2. Counter-regulatory PAI-1 elevation suppresses plasmin between harm episodes but fails to clear fully under chronic or repeated insult, producing per-cycle ratcheting of PAI-1 toward an entrenched ceiling. At ceiling, the system maintains sufficient residual plasmin for sustained PAR2 tone and chronic pain, while insufficient plasmin prevents ECM resolution or SPM generation — creating a dual neurological and fibrinolytic attractor. When infection occurs in this entrenched state, compressed fibrinolytic dynamic range converts an ordinarily self-limiting inflammatory response into an escalating LL-37-driven loop with sepsis-like characteristics. Genetic predisposition via the SERPINE1 4G/4G polymorphism establishes elevated PAI-1 baseline, accelerating ratchet progression. Chronic inflammation progressively demethylates the SERPINE1 promoter via TNF-alpha/TET1 signalling, epigenetically entrenching high PAI-1 expression independently of ongoing inflammatory stimulus. Aspirin's therapeutic action is reframed as phase-dependent ratchet interruption: AT-SPMs generated by acetylated COX-2 directly suppress PAI-1, restoring transient plasmin-mediated resolution capacity. The framework generates specific falsifiable predictions distinguishing it from existing models and identifies SERPINE1 methylation status as a candidate stratification biomarker for sepsis risk in chronically inflamed patient

titles.title: ReaxFF-guided optimization of VIRIP-based HIV‑1 entry inhibitors

descriptions.description: Peptides hold great promise for safe and effective treatment of viral infections. However, their use is often constrained by limited efficacy and high production costs, especially for long or complex peptide chains. Here, we used ReaxFF molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to optimize the size and activity of VIRIP (Virus Inhibitory Peptide), a naturally occurring 20-residue fragment of α1-antitrypsin that binds the HIV-1 GP41 fusion peptide (FP), thereby blocking viral fusion and entry into host cells. Specifically, we used the NMR structure of the complex between an optimized VIRIP derivative (VIR-165) and the HIV-1 gp41 FP for ReaxFF-guided in silico analysis, evaluating the contribution of each amino acid in the interaction of the inhibitor with its viral target. This approach allowed us to reduce the size of the HIV-1 FP inhibitor from 20 to 10 amino acids (2.28–1.11 kDa). HIV-1 infection assays showed that the size-optimized VIRIP derivative (soVIRIP) retains its broad-spectrum anti-HIV-1 capability and is nontoxic in the vertebrate zebrafish model. Compared to the original VIRIP, soVIRIP displayed more than 100-fold higher antiviral activity (IC50 of ∼120 nM). Thus, it is more potent than a dimeric 20-residue VIRIP derivative (VIR-576) that was proven safe and effective in a phase I/II clinical trial. Our results show that ReaxFF-based MD simulations represent a suitable approach for the optimization of therapeutic peptides.

titles.title: Increasing CO2 Levels and Carbonic Anhydrase Enzyme Orchestrate Skin Inflammation in Atopic Dermatitis

descriptions.description: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition in which epithelial barrier dysfunction and immune activation lead to eczema, with altered host-microbe interactions. Type-2 cytokines, such as IL-4 and IL-13, are established drivers of AD, yet the tissue interplay with IL-22 and environmental physio-chemical exposures remains incompletely defined. Indoor CO2 concentrations have increased in recent decades due to reduced ventilation and improved insulation, but whether CO2-linked physiopathological events can modulate AD-relevant skin inflammation is unclear. Carbonic anhydrases (CA) catalyze CO2 hydration and are central to tissue acid-base handling. Therefore, we hypothesized that elevated CO2 can affect and amplify type-2 inflammation through CA enzymes and downstream pro-inflammatory molecules in AD skin. To test this, we implemented ex-vivo human skin to capture full-thickness architecture and quantify barrier dysfunction as a tissue phenotype. Barrier integrity was quantified longitudinally by electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and integrated with transcriptomic and proteomic profiling. Human disease relevance was assessed using spatial transcriptomics of AD lesions and analyses of anti-IL4Rα-treated patients biopsies, and mechanistic probing included pharmacological inhibition and in vivo validation in the MC903-induced AD-like dermatitis model with single-cell RNA sequencing. The exposure to elevated indoor-relevant CO2 induced early barrier impairment in human skin and was associated with increased IL-13 levels. We identified CA2 as a candidate mediator. CA2 was induced by CO2 exposure and enriched in the epidermis of inflamed human skin. Pharmacological inhibition with the CA2-inhibitor, brinzolamide, attenuated IL-13-associated barrier dysfunction in ex-vivo skin and its production in the skin. CA2 inhibition also reduced clinical features and keratinocyte activation in MC903 dermatitis, supporting a CO2-CA axis as a testable environmental contributor to AD-like inflammation. In our further studies focusing the details of the type 2 response, IL-4, IL-13, and IL-22 each disrupt epithelial barrier integrity in ex-vivo skin and downregulated barrier pathways, while showing distinct immune profiles. In human native skin, IL-4/IL-13 suppressed antimicrobial peptide signatures, whereas IL-22 induced innate defense modules. Receptor-level cross-regulation (type-2 cytokines reducing IL22Rα1 and IL-22 increasing IL4Rα) supported cytokine interaction logic in the skin. Proteomics confirmed reduced abundance of key barrier proteins, particularly filaggrin and claudin-1. Finally, anti-IL4Rα-treated patient biopsies showed preferential normalization of IL-4/IL-13-associated genes with limited effects on IL-22-related genes. Collectively, this thesis supports a context-dependent model in which environmental and physicochemical conditions (CO2/CA2) and AD-related cytokines converge together to shape epithelial state. Taken together, these findings position skin barrier defects in AD as a dynamic skin output shaped by environmental, immune and physio-chemical contexts, motivating targeted studies to define exposure-response relationships and to test whether CA2-directed interventions may be targetable for AD.

titles.title: Genome and Transcriptome Mining of Macrocyclic Plant Peptide Natural Products for Multi-omics guided Drug Discovery

descriptions.description: Plants serve as a prolific source of novel structures for drug discovery. The identification of bioactive plant natural products through laboratory-based methods remains challenging and labor-intensive due to the inherent complexity of plant chemistry. Consequently, there is a critical need for effective strategies to enable in silico prediction of the structures and bioactivities of plant-derived compounds. With the increasing availability of plant genetic data and structural biology models of drug targets, this project seeks to develop a computational pipeline to predict bioactive compounds from plants by (a) identifying biosynthetically feasible molecules from plant genes in diverse genetic databases and (b) conducting both in silico and in vitro evaluation of predicted plant natural products against relevant human diseases. The long-term objective is to establish a plant genome mining strategy that streamlines the prediction of bioactive natural products from plant biosynthetic genes. Ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are produced as precursor peptides encoded by structural genes containing a core peptide region that undergoes modification and is subsequently released as the mature peptide. The primary compound class targeted in this project is burpitides, which are side-chain-macrocyclic plant RiPPs derived from BURP-domain-peptide cyclases. Mining plant genomes for peptide cyclases responsible for burpitide biosynthesis enables (a) prediction of chemical structures from precursor gene sequences, (b) in silico macrocyclic sampling and screening based on medicinal chemistry profiles bordering Lipinski’s rule of 5, and (c) scaffold diversification to facilitate expanded in vitro screening. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) represents an underexplored resource for large-scale, gene-guided discovery of plant bioactive peptides from fused burpitide cyclase pathways. The underlying rationale is that in silico analysis of plant genetic resources, when applied to rational drug discovery of diverse plant peptides, will yield new pharmacologically relevant lead structures for plant-derived therapeutics to treat human diseases. Benchmarking de novo RNA-seq assembly tools transformed thousands of public datasets from non-model organisms into a searchable database of 27,224 full-length, non-redundant BURP-domain sequences for biosynthetic gene discovery and the identification of fused moroidin cyclases, with 46 novel stephanotic acid-type burpitide cores from 17 plant species. This approach enabled the identification of new post-translational modifications in plant RiPP biosynthesis, including the isolation of glechomanin (Val-Trp crosslink) and mercurialin (Phe-Try crosslink), the discovery of moroidin-QLLVWRNH with a 5-fold improvement in bioactivity against H1437 lung adenocarcinoma cells, and the expansion of chemotaxonomic knowledge of moroidins across diverse plant families. RNA-Seq analysis, integrated with knowledge graph-driven agentic artificial intelligence, guided preliminary deconvolution of the mechanism of action for moroidin-QLLVWRNH. In silico library curation of 375 two- and three-dimensional structures enabled structure-based virtual screening against lipoprotein signal peptidase II (LspA), a cyclic peptide antimicrobial target. This docking enabled the computational discovery of a lyciumin hit candidate, QPFGVFRW. Expression of BURP-domain precursor genes in Nicotiana benthamiana provided a source-plant-independent biosynthesis strategy for accessing macrocyclic peptides. Additionally, the cultivation and extraction of seedling tissues from diverse plant species broadened metabolomic coverage by generating 1169 full MS/MS spectra, enabling the identification of lyciumin metabolites in nightshade stems and beet roots. This will enable future integration with publicly available plant genomes for natural product discovery. This research advances the understanding of plant peptide chemistry and its application in rational drug design through plant genome mining.

titles.title: Petibiotics; developing antimicrobial agents for Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus

descriptions.description:
Probiotic strains, encompassing Lactobacillus plantarum PTCC 1896, two distinct strains of L. plantarum procured from local dairy farms in East Azerbaijan, Iran, L. paracasei IRBC-M 10784, L. acidophilus PTCC-1932, and L. rhamnosus IRBC-M 10782, were subjected to a prolonged exposure to a lysate of Escherichia coli ATCC 25922 and Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213. The pathogenic microorganisms underwent inactivation via heat treatment at 70 °C for a duration of 50 minutes, subsequently followed by an immediate transfer to an ice-water bath to induce a thermal shock response. These probiotics, designated as petibiotics, demonstrated a pronounced enhancement in antibacterial efficacy. A proteomic analysis employing LC–MS/MS techniques was conducted to elucidate alterations in the protein expression profiles between the exposed (petibiotic) and the unexposed probiotic strains.

The proteomic identification phase was executed by extracting proteins utilizing a RIPA lysis kit in accordance with the manufacturer’s specifications. Initially, bacterial cell suspensions (both exposed and unexposed) in MRS broth were transferred into Eppendorf tubes and subjected to centrifugation for 5 minutes at an acceleration of 1000 rpm. Following this, the supernatant was discarded. The resultant pellet was subsequently resuspended in cold PBS and centrifuged once more at 1000 rpm, after which the supernatant was again discarded. An adequate volume of RIPA lysis buffer containing a protease inhibitor was introduced to the cell pellet. Upon resuspension, the pellet was vortexed for 15 seconds and incubated on ice at 4°C for 30 minutes, with intermittent vortexing for 15 seconds every 10 minutes. Thereafter, the samples underwent centrifugation at 4°C for 15 minutes at 13000 rpm. The supernatants from all samples were collected and transferred into cryotubes, which were subsequently dispatched to the Department of Chemistry at the University of Copenhagen, Denmark, for enzymatic digestion and protein identification. Proteins were subjected to digestion utilizing trypsin and subsequently analyzed via LC-MS/MS. Identification of the proteins was facilitated by Mascot software (Matrix Science, London, UK) through the selection of the mass peptide fingerprint component. The SwissProt database was employed for reference, with trypsin designated as the protein digestion enzyme and Firmicutes (gram-positive bacteria) as the taxonomy. Carbamidomethyl (C) was established as the fixed modification, while oxidation (M) and acetyl (protein N-term) were considered as variable modifications for the protein modification type. The probability score (95% confidence level) computed by the software was utilized as the criterion for precise identification, and to validate the presence of proteins in Lactobacillus, the BLASTp tool was employed within the NCBI nr database.

titles.title: Visualizing a lung neutrophil-platelet immunothrombosis cascade during sepsis in mice

descriptions.description:
Sepsis is an immune paradox where host defence is necessary for survival
 but also contributes to organ damage and death. Using lung intravital
 microscopy we defined an immunothrombosis cascade of neutrophil and
 platelets in the microcirculation in response to E. coli sepsis.
 Neutrophil cathelicidin localized neutrophils to E. coli and initiated
 founder immunothrombi via formyl-peptide receptors. Immunothrombi captured
 vascular bacteria and cathelicidin enabled antimicrobial activities in
 platelets. Blocking cathelicidin prevented the immunothrombosis cascade
 and attenuated early sepsis death but resulted in delayed death with
 uncontrolled infection. LTB4 amplified the immunothrombi and inhibiting it
 diminished detrimental immunothrombi while preserving host defense, thus
 representing a discrete inflection point of sepsis disease progression.
 Therefore, targeting the immunothrombi cascade can mitigate
 immunopathology without suppressing host defence during sepsis.

# Visualizing a lung neutrophil-platelet immunothrombosis cascade during
 sepsis in mice Dataset DOI:
 [10.5061/dryad.0k6djhbfz](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.0k6djhbfz) ##
 Description of the data and file structure Neutrophil behavior was
 characterized using Imaris software (Oxford Instruments, v10.1). In brief,
 surfaces were applied to corresponding channels with absolute intensity
 thresholding. Voxels <40 were filtered out for neutrophils, and <10
 for platelets, and endothelium. Spots were used for tracking bacteria.
 Neutrophil cellular characteristics, including area, sphericity
 (polarization), platelet surface overlap, distance to *E. coli,* etc.,
 were measured. 2D video imaging was used for cellular behavioral analysis
 in the pulmonary microvasculature. Imaris surface and track parameters of
 neutrophils were exported with specific raw values into Microsoft Excel.
 Extracted raw values of morphometric and kinematic parameters of interest
 were exported into .csv files and loaded into R (v4.2.0). To facilitate
 ‘track-back’ analysis of cluster behaviors, unique neutrophil surface
 identification signatures (NeuID) along with unique animal IDs and
 genotypes were imprinted into the metadata and were maintained throughout
 the data analysis workflow. ### Files and variables #### File:
 Neutrophil_Behavioromics_adv0377_Brown_et_al.xlsx
 **Description:** Descriptions of Imaris measurements can be found in the
 Imaris Reference
 Manual: [https://www.bitplane.com/download/manuals/ReferenceManual9_2_0.pdf](https://www.bitplane.com/download/manuals/ReferenceManual9_2_0.pdf) ##### Variables * Area (µm^2^) * Displacement delta length (µm) * Ellipticity oblate (AU) * Platelet overlap (µm^2^) * Distance to *E. coli *(µm) * Distance to platelets (µm) * Speed (µm/s) * Polarization (sphericity) (AU) ## Code/software Selected parameters were integrated into a single .csv file which was run through the Seurat (v.5.1.0) pipeline for data analysis. For analysis of the immunothrombi dataset, we transformed the original matrix into a Seurat object and normalized and scaled the parameters. We performed a principal component analysis and the cells were clustered based on *k*-nearest neighbor graphs using the Louvain algorithm. Finally, a non-linear reduction technique (*t*-SNE and UMAP) was performed to visualize the data in a low-dimensional space. Graphs were created using ggplot2. ## Access information Other publicly accessible locations of the data: * NA Data was derived from the following sources: * NA

titles.title: Machine Learning Models for Antimicrobial Peptide Classification Using k-mer Sequence Representations

descriptions.description: This paper was completed as part of the Young Scholars Research Program.

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short amino acid sequences that play a critical role in immune defenses and have gained attention as potential alternatives to traditional antibiotics. Due to the difficulty of experimentally identifying new AMPs, machine learning approaches have been explored as a method for predicting antimicrobial activity from peptide sequences. In this study, baseline machine learning models were applied to classify peptide sequences as antimicrobial or non-antimicrobial using simple sequence-based feature representations. Peptide sequences were converted into numerical features using a k-mer bag-of-words approach and used to train logistic regression and random forest classifiers. Model performance was evaluated on a held-out test set using confusion matrix analysis and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Both models demonstrated performance close to random guessing, with accuracy values near 50% and ROC area under the curve values close to 0.5. These results indicate that baseline machine learning models using k-mer sequence features alone are insufficient for reliably predicting antimicrobial peptides. This study highlights the need for more advanced feature representations and modeling approaches to improve predictive performance in antimicrobial peptide classification.
